journal_name: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems

abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel algebraic framework for logic synthesis that fundamentally reconceptualizes Boolean network optimization through the lens of tropical geometry. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on heuristic search or Boolean algebra manipulation, our paradigm treats logic networks as tropical semirings, enabling exact characterization of synthesis boundaries and optimality conditions. We prove that the minimum literal count problem in two-level logic can be solved via tropical polytope projection, and extend this result to multi-level network optimization through a new concept of tropical circuit depth. The theoretical contribution lies in establishing a polynomial-time computable bound on synthesis quality that was previously considered intractable. Experimental results on benchmark circuits demonstrate that our framework produces solutions that match or exceed those obtained by state-of-the-art ABC synthesis while providing theoretical guarantees on optimality gaps. This work opens a new research direction at the intersection of tropical algebra and VLSI design automation, suggesting that many classical synthesis problems admit elegant geometric interpretations. The proposed framework is particularly significant for emerging technologies where traditional heuristics fail to provide predictable results, establishing a mathematically rigorous foundation for next-generation logic synthesis tools.

This paper presents rigorous theoretical analysis that significantly improves timing closure for modern VLSI designs through a new statistical timing model based on order statistics. We derive tighter bounds on the worst-case delay distribution in sequential circuits by exploiting the correlation structure among timing paths that existing SSTA methods neglect. Our key theoretical contribution is a novel characterization of the maximum delay among correlated paths using extreme value theory, which yields closed-form expressions for guardband computation under realistic correlation assumptions. We prove that the conventional independence assumption in path-based statistical timing analysis introduces systematic underestimation errors that grow superlinearly with design complexity. The proposed model reduces the required timing margin by 23-31% compared to industry-standard libraries while maintaining the same statistical confidence level. Furthermore, we provide exact complexity analysis showing that our approach achieves quadratic speedup over Monte Carlo simulation for circuits with up to 10^5 timing paths. These theoretical results are validated through extensive experiments on ISCAS and ITC benchmarks, demonstrating that the proposed framework enables more aggressive circuit optimization without compromising yield targets.

This paper presents NeuROM, a paradigm-shifting framework that integrates neural network topology optimization directly into the physical design flow for heterogeneous system-level integration. Unlike conventional approaches that treat architecture exploration and physical implementation as sequential stages, NeuROM jointly optimizes computational graph structure, functional unit allocation, and physical layout through an end-to-end differentiable design space exploration engine. The system introduces the concept of differentiable floorplanning, where placement decisions are optimized simultaneously with operator fusion and memory hierarchy design using gradient-based optimization. NeuROM generates highly optimized layouts for chiplet-based systems that achieve 3.2x improvement in interconnect bandwidth and 47% reduction in total wirelength compared to current practice. The framework supports automatic generation of RTL, physical design constraints, and verification testbenches from the unified specification. Key innovations include a learned cost model trained on 50,000 historical designs that accurately predicts timing, power, and area across different process nodes, and a multi-objective Pareto optimizer that enables designers to navigate complex tradeoffs interactively. This work establishes a new design methodology where machine learning accelerators are co-designed with their own implementation tools, fundamentally changing how system-level design automation is performed.

This paper presents RapidPlace, a high-performance placement engine that achieves substantial improvements in solution quality and runtime for advanced-node designs through hierarchical optimization with learned cost models. The system introduces a novel multi-level architecture that combines coarse-grained global placement with fine-grained detailed placement through learned refinement operators. RapidPlace incorporates physics-inspired force-directed placement enhanced with graph neural networks that predict wirelength gradients with 94% accuracy, reducing optimization iterations by 65% compared to EDA-Industry-standard tools. A key contribution is the development of an efficient GPU-accelerated quadratic placement solver that processes designs with 10^9 routed segments in under 2 hours, representing a 12x speedup over prior art while achieving 8% better total wirelength. The system addresses critical challenges in advanced-node physical design including design rule checking awareness during placement and electromigration-aware current density optimization. Experimental results on 45nm through 5nm process nodes demonstrate consistent improvements across all major benchmarks, with an average 15% reduction in total negative slack and 22% improvement in power delivery network impedance. RapidPlace has been integrated into a production design flow and used to tape out 23 chips across various application domains.
